title: Compute & scaling
oneLiner: Buy by pattern (Spot if it can be interrupted, a Savings Plan if it's steady), bake slow installs into a golden AMI, pick the load balancer by layer (ALB HTTP, NLB TCP/UDP), and let a launch template drive the ASG.

notes.html: Ask the questions in order: can it be interrupted, does it need its own server, is it steady for years? The first yes is the answer. Mixing is normal: a Savings Plan for the baseline, Spot or On-Demand for peaks.

notes.html: Pick by layer. HTTP features (paths, hosts, headers) mean ALB. Raw TCP/UDP or a fixed IP means NLB. Third-party appliances inline means GWLB.

items: Sticky sessions keep a user on one target; they don't survive that target dying. For real fault tolerance store sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB.
Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB, off by default for NLB (and NLB charges for cross-AZ traffic when on).

questions.q: An Auto Scaling group must run a baseline of On-Demand instances and add Spot instances across several instance types. Which setup needs the least operational effort?

options.t: A launch template with a mixed instances policy on one ASG
options.why: Launch templates support several types and an On-Demand/Spot split in a single group.

options.t: A launch configuration listing the instance types
options.why: Launch configurations allow one instance type and no Spot/On-Demand mix.

options.t: Two ASGs, one On-Demand and one Spot, behind the same ALB
options.why: Works, but it's two groups to keep in step. More effort.

options.t: A Spot Fleet next to the ASG, managed by a Lambda function
options.why: Custom glue for something the ASG does natively.

questions.q: Which statement about EC2 launch configurations is true today?

options.t: They can be edited in place to change the AMI
options.why: They're immutable. You'd create a new one.

options.t: Accounts created after October 2024 can't create them, and launch templates replace them
options.why: AWS stopped new launch configurations; launch templates add versions and mixed instances.

options.t: They support versions, so an ASG can roll back
options.why: Versions are a launch template feature.

options.t: They're required to use Spot instances in an ASG
options.why: Spot mixes need a launch template.

questions.q: An ASG's new instances take 15 minutes to serve traffic because user data installs packages and the app. Traffic spikes come fast. What's the most effective fix?

options.t: Bake the packages and app into a golden AMI and use it in the launch template
options.why: Nothing left to install at boot, so instances are ready in a minute or two.

options.t: Use a larger instance type
options.why: Installs a bit faster, still minutes of downloads.

options.t: Increase the scaling cooldown
options.why: Slows scaling further.

options.t: Move the install script into a launch lifecycle hook
options.why: Still installs at boot; the hook only holds the instance while it does.

questions.q: Dev, test and prod run the same application. Only the database endpoint and log level differ per environment. Which approach has the least operational overhead?

options.t: One golden AMI, with user data reading per-environment values from Parameter Store at boot
options.why: One image to patch; small differences come in at boot.

options.t: Build a separate AMI for each environment
options.why: Three images to build and patch for a few settings.

options.t: Hard-code all three endpoints in the app and pick one by hostname
options.why: Brittle, and a config change needs a redeploy.

options.t: Launch from a base AMI and have engineers SSH in to configure each instance
options.why: Manual and doesn't scale.

questions.q: A multiplayer game uses UDP. Players' networks allowlist the server by a fixed IP in each AZ. Which load balancer fits?

options.t: Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP per AZ
options.why: Layer 4, supports UDP, and gives a static IP per AZ.

options.t: Application Load Balancer
options.why: HTTP/HTTPS only, and no static IP.

options.t: Gateway Load Balancer
options.why: For inline appliances, not serving clients.

options.t: CloudFront in front of EC2
options.why: CloudFront serves HTTP(S), not raw UDP game traffic.

questions.q: One domain must send /api/* to containers and /images/* to another fleet, using the fewest resources.

options.t: One ALB with path-based listener rules to two target groups
options.why: Layer-7 rules route by path on one load balancer.

options.t: One NLB with two listeners
options.why: NLB routes by port, it can't see URL paths.

options.t: Two NLBs and Route 53 weighted records
options.why: DNS can't route by path either, and it's more resources.

options.t: A Gateway Load Balancer
options.why: For appliances, not HTTP routing.

questions.q: Security wants all traffic entering a VPC to pass through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances that scales and stays highly available. What should they use?

options.t: Gateway Load Balancer with the appliances as targets
options.why: Built for transparent, scalable inline inspection.

options.t: Network Load Balancer in front of the appliances
options.why: Doesn't insert itself transparently into routing like GWLB does.

options.t: Security groups on every instance
options.why: Not deep inspection, and not a third-party appliance.

options.t: AWS WAF on the ALB
options.why: Only HTTP rules on that ALB, not all traffic.

questions.q: A Kafka cluster of 60 brokers must survive a rack failure, stay rack-aware, and use three AZs. Which placement fits?

options.t: One partition placement group spread over the three AZs
options.why: Partition groups span AZs, up to 7 partitions per AZ, and expose the partition to the app.

options.t: A cluster placement group
options.why: One AZ and shared hardware: one failure can hit many brokers.

options.t: A spread placement group
options.why: Max 7 instances per AZ, far too few for 60.

options.t: Three partition groups, one per AZ, since partitions can't span AZs
options.why: They can span AZs, so this adds groups for nothing.

questions.q: An HPC job needs the lowest network latency and highest throughput between 20 nodes. Fault tolerance isn't a concern.

options.t: Cluster placement group in one AZ
options.why: Packs nodes close together for low latency.

options.t: Spread placement group
options.why: Puts instances on separate hardware, the opposite goal.

options.t: Partition placement group across AZs
options.why: Cross-AZ adds latency.

options.t: Instances in three AZs behind an NLB
options.why: Spreads nodes apart.

questions.q: An account has 5 Elastic IPs in us-east-1 and none in eu-west-1. It needs 3 more in us-east-1. What's true?

options.t: Request a quota increase for us-east-1; the limit is 5 per region and can be raised
options.why: It's a soft limit per region.

options.t: The account is out of Elastic IPs in every region
options.why: The limit is per region, not per account.

options.t: 5 is a hard limit, so use auto-assigned public IPs
options.why: It can be raised, and auto-assigned IPs change on stop/start.

options.t: Allocate them in eu-west-1 and attach them to us-east-1 instances
options.why: Elastic IPs are regional.

questions.q: A nightly image-processing job can be stopped and resumed at any point and has no deadline. What's the most cost-effective option?

options.t: Spot Instances
options.why: Up to 90% off, and interruptions don't matter here.

options.t: Standard Reserved Instances
options.why: Pays for capacity 24/7 for a job that runs nightly.

options.t: On-Demand Instances
options.why: Works, but costs more than Spot.

options.t: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Most expensive, for licensing or compliance.

questions.q: Which statement about Convertible Reserved Instances is correct?

options.t: Up to about 66% off, and they can be exchanged for another family, OS or tenancy
options.why: That's the trade: less discount than Standard, more flexibility.

options.t: About 54% off and locked to one instance family
options.why: The discount is up to ~66%, and the family can be exchanged.

options.t: They can be sold on the RI Marketplace
options.why: Only Standard RIs can be sold.

options.t: They also cover Fargate and Lambda
options.why: Only a Compute Savings Plan does.

questions.q: A company will run steady EC2 for 3 years but plans to move part of it to Fargate and Lambda. Which commitment gives savings with the most flexibility?

options.t: Compute Savings Plan
options.why: Applies across EC2 families, regions, Fargate and Lambda.

options.t: EC2 Instance Savings Plan
options.why: One family in one region, and no Fargate or Lambda.

options.t: Standard Reserved Instances
options.why: Locked to instance attributes.

options.t: Convertible Reserved Instances
options.why: EC2 only, and exchanges need effort.

questions.q: Licensed software is billed per physical socket, and the company wants to bring its own licenses. Which option is required?

options.t: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: You see the sockets and cores, so licenses can be counted.

options.t: Dedicated Instances
options.why: Single-tenant, but no visibility of sockets.

options.t: Spot Instances
options.why: Shared hardware and interruptions.

options.t: A cluster placement group
options.why: Placement, not licensing.

questions.q: An app spends 20 minutes loading a large in-memory cache at start. It's stopped every night and must resume quickly in the morning.

options.t: Enable hibernation on the instance (encrypted root EBS)
options.why: RAM is saved to EBS and restored, so the cache is warm.

options.t: Stop and start normally
options.why: RAM is lost; the 20-minute warm-up repeats.

options.t: Store the cache on instance store
options.why: Instance store is wiped on stop.

options.t: Bake the cache into the AMI
options.why: The cache is built at runtime and changes; an AMI is static.

questions.q: Containerized jobs run nightly for about 2 hours each, from a queue. The team wants no servers to manage.

options.t: AWS Batch with a Fargate compute environment
options.why: Batch queues and runs the jobs; Fargate removes servers.

options.t: Lambda functions triggered by EventBridge
options.why: 15-minute limit.

options.t: AWS Batch is EC2-only, so run ECS on Fargate with a custom scheduler
options.why: Batch supports Fargate, so no custom scheduler is needed.

options.t: EC2 Spot instances with cron
options.why: Servers to manage.

questions.q: A Lambda function attached to private subnets must call a public third-party API. It currently times out. What fixes it?

options.t: Route the private subnets to a NAT gateway in a public subnet
options.why: Lambda in a VPC has no public IP; NAT gives it outbound internet.

options.t: Attach an internet gateway to the Lambda function
options.why: IGWs attach to VPCs, and Lambda ENIs get no public IP.

options.t: Create a VPC interface endpoint for the API
options.why: Endpoints are for AWS or PrivateLink services, not any public API.

options.t: Increase the function timeout
options.why: It will still have no route out.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive API on Lambda shows slow first requests after quiet periods. Which fixes it with the least code change?

options.t: Provisioned concurrency
options.why: Keeps initialized environments ready, so no cold start.

options.t: Reserved concurrency
options.why: Caps or guarantees concurrency; doesn't pre-warm.

options.t: Move the function into a VPC
options.why: Doesn't remove cold starts.

options.t: Raise the timeout
options.why: Timeout isn't the problem.

questions.q: ECS tasks on Fargate must read objects from an S3 bucket. Where do the permissions go?

options.t: The ECS task role
options.why: The role the app's AWS calls use.

options.t: The task execution role
options.why: Only for pulling images and writing logs on the task's behalf.

options.t: An EC2 instance profile
options.why: Fargate has no instance you control, and it'd be shared by all tasks.

options.t: Access keys in environment variables
options.why: Long-lived keys; avoid.

questions.q: Instances in an ASG pass EC2 status checks but the app returns HTTP 500s. The ALB marks them unhealthy, yet the ASG never replaces them.

options.t: Turn on ELB health checks for the ASG
options.why: By default the ASG only uses EC2 status checks.

options.t: Increase the health check grace period
options.why: Delays checks; doesn't change which checks count.

options.t: Add a CloudWatch alarm to reboot instances
options.why: Reboots don't replace, and it's extra glue.

options.t: Change the termination policy
options.why: Decides which instance goes on scale-in, not health.

Read a DB endpoint from Parameter Store
Register with a config server at boot
Same in every environment, slow to install
